subject: Biology
title: Short-Term vs Long-Term Memory
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Short-Term vs Long-Term Memory.

hook.text: Your short-term memory holds about seven items for roughly 30 seconds. Then it fades.

buildup.text: Working memory is the brain's scratchpad—it holds and manipulates information during tasks.

discovery.text: Long-term memory has virtually no capacity limit. It can store information for a lifetime.

twist.text: Sleep plays a critical role. During deep sleep, the brain replays and consolidates new memories.

climax.text: Without consolidation, today's experiences would fade by tomorrow—sleep turns them permanent.

punchline.text: Study, then sleep. That's how memories stick.

quiz.question: When does the brain consolidate new memories?

details.summary: Short-term memory holds about 7 items for 20 to 30 seconds, while long-term memory stores unlimited information potentially for a lifetime. Transfer from short-term to long-term requires consolidation through repetition, emotional significance, or meaningful association.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding memory systems explains why cramming fails, why emotional events are unforgettable, and how brain injuries can selectively destroy the ability to form new memories while leaving old ones intact.
takeaways: Short-term memory is limited to roughly 7 items for under 30 seconds
Long-term memory has essentially unlimited capacity and duration
Consolidation transfers information from short-term to long-term storage

faq.question: What is the difference between short-term and working memory?
faq.answer: Short-term memory passively holds information briefly. Working memory actively manipulates that information, like rearranging numbers in your head to do mental math. Working memory is short-term memory plus active cognitive processing.

faq.question: Why can some brain-injured patients remember the past but not form new memories?
faq.answer: The hippocampus is required for consolidating new short-term memories into long-term storage. Damage to the hippocampus prevents new memory formation while leaving existing long-term memories stored elsewhere in the cortex intact.
